claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo contains 20 at% each of Nb, Zr, Ti, Hf, and Mo.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited room-temperature plasticity.
The high Mo content of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo increases the electronegativity difference among its constituents.
The Mo-associated electronegativity difference restricts plasticity by limiting dislocation mobility.
The proposed intervention changes the composition to Nb20Zr20Ti20Hf20Mo15Ta5 in atomic percent.
The modified six-element composition maintains an overall equiatomic balance.
Replacing 5 at% Mo with 5 at% Ta will reduce the overall electronegativity mismatch.
The modified alloy will retain a single-phase disordered BCC solid solution.
Adding Ta will alter the alloy's lattice distortion.
Reducing electronegativity mismatch will weaken strong directional bonds.
Weakening the directional bonds will facilitate dislocation motion and activate more slip systems.
More active dislocation motion and slip will improve room-temperature compressive plasticity.
Ta has an atomic size sufficiently similar to Mo to preserve strengthening lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion underpins the high strength of this alloy.
The modified alloy will retain a compressive yield strength near 1719 MPa.
The modified alloy will have greater room-temperature compressive plastic strain than equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The beneficial strength-plasticity effect is expected around a 25% relative reduction in Mo content with corresponding Ta addition.
Larger composition changes may destabilize the disordered BCC phase or produce secondary phases.

contradictions.description: The intervention says that the overall equiatomic balance is retained, but the stated modified composition is Nb20Zr20Ti20Hf20Mo15Ta5, which is not equiatomic across its six elements.

The predicted outcome requires only a measurable increase in plastic strain, whereas the falsification rule effectively requires at least a 5% increase; a measurable increase below 5% could therefore satisfy the prediction while still being classified as falsification.
